newsitem.title: UK: Brazil's Malan slams critics of trade performance.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Malan slams critics of trade performance.

text.p: Brazilian finance minister Pedro Malan on Thursday mounted a vigorous defence of his country's recent trade performance, slamming critics who have said October's hefty trade deficit was the start of a trend.

"When the figures for November come up shortly they will show that October was a peculiar month, for a variety of reasons," Malan told a London conference on Latin America's Mercosur trade bloc, adding that special and seasonal factors had weighed in the October result.
"We are not concerned at all and we don't think people should engage in naive and mechanical statistical exercises multiplying that (October) figure by 12 and saying it is a trend," he said.

Brazil's trade account is caught in the pincer of sluggish exports and an import boom fuelled by strong economic growth, but the country still shocked financial markets when its October trade deficit came in at a worse than expected $1.3 billion.
Some foreign investors, still nervous in the wake of the 1994 Mexican crisis, have produced deficit projections of $4.0 billion for 1996 and $6.0 for 1997 in the wake of that figure.
But Malan said that the annual trade deficit was likely to amount to less than three percent of GDP and posed no problem to Brazil's finances.
"It is financeable -- 2.8 percent of GDP is easily financeable," he said.
Kleinwort Benson analyst Neil Dougall said that, were Brazil's trade position still to show signs of weakness into the early part of 1997, only minor adjustments would be needed.
"The most that would be required would be a minor adjustment in monetary policy," he said.
He agreed with the Brazilian view that the trade problem was perhaps just a temporary one, with seasonal factors accounting for the unusually high October figure.
Some economists have been speculating on whether Brazil will need to step up import tariffs, raise interest rates or tighten consumer credit to even up the trade imbalance.

But Malan insisted Brazil was not planning to take any hasty action following the October number, which some analysts say was boosted by rising oil prices and a pre-Christmas surge in imports of consumer goods.
"We don't feel there is any need to take any precipitous action whatsoever," Malan said.

He said Brazil was now a net importer of capital, after the country's hyperinflationary past when it had been a capital exporter, and that it was normal for capital importing countries to sustain current account deficits.
And he quashed some investors' obsession with constant trade surpluses.
"A healthy economy does not need to post enormous trade surpluses," he said.

"This is absolutely wrong. The situation in Brazil has changed completely -- we have renegotiated our debt, we have no capital flight, there is no need to have a policy geared to generating mega trade surpluses."
He denied the Brazilian economy was growing too fast, fuelling consumer demand, after preliminary figures indicated third quarter year-on-year GDP growth of 7.0 percent.
The government is still predicting an annual figure of 3.0 percent this year, and 4.5 percent in 1997.
"There is no overheating," he said.
